rules.rule:
User interface. The built-in TypeScript rules already cover hook misuse, render side effects and
over-memoisation; this is what they do not.

## Accessibility

There is no accessibility linter in this project, and around fifty UI files write `aria`
attributes by hand. Review is therefore the only guard.

- Every interactive element must be reachable and operable by keyboard. Flag a `div` or `span`
  with `onClick` and no role, `tabIndex` and key handler — a native `button` is almost always the
  correct fix rather than adding three attributes.
- Flag an input without a programmatic label, an icon-only control without an accessible name, and
  an image without `alt` (empty `alt` is correct for decoration, and should be explicit).
- Flag a dialog or menu that does not trap focus and restore it on close.
- Flag state conveyed by colour alone, and a disabled control with no explanation of why.
- Flag `aria-*` on an element whose native semantics already say the same thing; a wrong ARIA
  attribute is worse than none.

## Text belongs in the locale files

This app has an i18n setup with locale files.

- Flag a user-facing string written literally in a component.
- Flag a sentence assembled by concatenating fragments; word order differs between languages.
- Flag a date, number or currency formatted by hand rather than through the locale.

## Behaviour under failure and delay
- Every asynchronous view needs a loading state and an error state. A spinner that never resolves
  and a blank panel are the two most common ways this is got wrong.
- An empty result and a failed request must not render the same thing: one says there is nothing,
  the other that we do not know.
- Flag a destructive action with no confirmation, and a confirmation whose wording does not say
  what will be lost.
- Flag a form that can be submitted twice.


## Reuse before you build

The web application keeps around eighty shared components in `shared/ui` — button, card, modal,
popover, confirm dialog, data table header, avatar, action menu and the rest. A screen that
hand-rolls one of these looks almost right, behaves differently under keyboard and screen
readers, and drifts further every time either copy is touched.

- Before accepting a new component, check `shared/ui` for one that already does the job. If a
  close match exists, say which, and prefer extending it with a prop over a second implementation.
- Flag a raw `<button>`, `<input>`, `<select>`, `<table>` or hand-built dialog, dropdown, tooltip
  or tab strip where a shared component exists.
- Flag a component added to a feature folder that is plainly generic — no feature-specific props,
  no feature imports. It belongs in `shared/ui` where the next screen can find it.
- Flag the reverse too: a feature-specific concern pushed into `shared/ui`, which makes a shared
  component know about one screen.
- Where a shared component is extended, flag a new prop that duplicates an existing one with a
  different name.

## Design tokens, not literal values

This project already enforces some of this with ratchet tests over raw hex, the type scale and the
brand palette, so a finding here should be consistent with them rather than argue against them.

- Flag a literal colour, including hex, `rgb()` and named colours, where a token exists.
- Flag a hand-picked font size, weight, line height or spacing value that sits outside the scale.
  Arbitrary spacing is what makes two pages feel like two products.
- Flag a hardcoded breakpoint, radius, shadow or z-index; z-index especially, since competing
  values cause layering bugs that only appear once both components are on screen.

## Consistency across pages

- The same action should use the same words everywhere. Flag a button reading `Delete` beside an
  equivalent one reading `Remove`, and a dialog whose primary action is worded differently from
  its siblings.
- Flag a layout that departs from comparable pages without a stated reason — where the title,
  filters and primary action sit is part of the product, not a per-page decision.
- Flag an empty, loading or error state styled differently from the shared one.
- Flag a new icon introduced for a meaning an existing icon already carries.
